title: Join Us
text:
We welcome collaborators and applicants interested in AI-enabled multi-hazard forecasting, early warning systems, and decision support.
Our work combines machine learning, physical modelling, and uncertainty analysis to support risk-informed decisions for natural hazards.

title: Join Us
text:
Opportunities

TREES DLA PhD projects — 2027 entry
Applications are open through the TREES Doctoral Landscape Award. The application deadline is 14 December 2026 at 17:00 UK time.

  
    PhD · CASE partnership with BGS
    Quantifying Landslide Impacts across Europe using AI
    Develop AI and Earth observation methods to map landslides across Europe and investigate their contribution to disaster impacts and multi-hazard risk.
    Supervisors: Faith Taylor and Lorenzo Nava, King’s College London.Co-supervisors: Alessandro Novellino and Ekbal Hussain, British Geological Survey (BGS). Includes a BGS placement of at least three months.
    Official project description ↗
  
  
    PhD · AI and cascading hazards
    Predicting Extreme Geohazard Flows with AI
    Combine satellite, terrain, seismic and environmental data to reconstruct and predict long-runout flows, including debris flows and glacial lake outburst floods.
    Supervisors: Tom Matthews and Lorenzo Nava, King’s College London.Co-supervisor: Max Van Wyk de Vries, University of Cambridge.
    Official project description ↗
  

How to apply: follow the TREES application guidance for eligibility, funding arrangements and the application portal. Advertised projects use Route 1; applicants can select up to three projects. Studentships are awarded through the TREES selection process.
TREES funding covers a stipend and UK-rate fees. A limited number of international studentships also cover overseas fees, subject to funding availability; consult the official guidance for the conditions that apply to you.
For project enquiries, email lorenzo.nava@kcl.ac.uk. Applications must be submitted through TREES.

title: About
text: The Multi-Hazard Intelligence Lab (MHIL) at King’s College London studies how artificial intelligence can support hazard forecasting, early warning, and disaster response.

title: About
text:
Research focus
Our current research centres on landslides and cascading hazards: detecting and mapping events from satellite data, forecasting displacement and failure, and modelling runout and spatial impact. These projects provide the foundation for a broader research agenda in multi-hazard forecasting and decision support.
We are interested in how hazards interact, how uncertainty can be represented in predictions, and how those predictions can inform decisions before and after an event. See our research projects for the specific questions, methods, and applications we are working on.

title: About
text:
Our approach
We combine machine learning, Earth observation, and physical–statistical modelling. Current projects use SAR and multispectral imagery, monitoring time series, and terrain data to investigate hazard detection, forecasting, and cascading processes.
Our wider research agenda includes uncertainty-aware evaluation, early warning systems, and the connection between model outputs and disaster response decisions.

title: About
text:
At King’s College London
MHIL brings together research interests in artificial intelligence, Earth systems, and disaster risk, spanning the King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Department of Geography.
The lab is led by Lorenzo Nava, an AI+ Academic Senior Fellow at King’s College London. Meet Lorenzo, the co-supervised researchers, and collaborators on the People page.

title: People
text:
AI+ Academic Senior Fellow at King's College London
    Lorenzo Nava
    
      Deep Learning, Remote Sensing, and Numerical Modelling for geohazard prediction and response
    
  

I am an AI+ Academic Senior Fellow at King’s College London, working on the use of artificial intelligence for disaster forecasting, modelling, and response.
My research focuses on interacting natural hazards, with an emphasis on AI-enabled forecasting, early warning systems, and decision support for disaster risk reduction. I develop machine learning approaches combined with system-level modelling to better understand cascading impacts, uncertainty, and operational constraints in real-world settings.
My work sits at the interface of artificial intelligence, Earth systems, and disaster risk, spanning the King’s Institute for Artificial Intelligence and the Department of Geography.
